periods.analysis: Program cost recovery closed 2024-Q3 at 46.6%, comfortably above the 40% target and giving us room to keep fees reasonable while protecting access. This quarter’s performance was helped by full summer camp enrollment at Harborview Recreation Center, strong lap-lane rentals at Mariner Pool, and steady meeting-room bookings at the Central Library. The important resident outcome is that earned revenue is carrying a healthy share of program cost without pushing families out of the programs they rely on.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the summer operating playbook by opening 2025 camp preregistration first for returning scholarship families, then expanding public registration by site capacity. Ask Recreation and Libraries finance staff to review the top 20 fee-based offerings and confirm that instructor contracts, supply costs, and waiver usage are being coded consistently before the next seasonal catalog is finalized.

periods.analysis: Cost recovery remained green at 42.3%, down 4.3 points from 46.6% in 2024-Q3, which is a normal seasonal step-down as outdoor rentals taper and holiday closures reduce class days. The drop was most visible in evening aquatics and community-room rentals, while youth enrichment at Eastbank Library and senior fitness at Bayfront Community Center continued to hold steady. I am pleased that we stayed above target while still honoring fee waivers and reduced-price access for households facing Harborview’s broader affordability pressures.
periods.recommendations: Keep the winter mix balanced by bundling lower-cost library workshops with paid recreation classes in the January catalog. Have site managers at Mariner Pool and Bayfront Community Center test two additional Friday evening rental blocks, but only where staffing can be covered without overtime pressure.

periods.analysis: In 2025-Q1, cost recovery improved to 45.1%, up 2.8 points from 42.3% in 2024-Q4, and stayed solidly green. The rebound reflects better winter class fill rates, especially youth swim lessons, adult ceramics at the West Harbor Arts Room, and paid technology clinics at Central Library. This is the kind of operating result residents should expect from us: more seats filled, fewer cancellations, and a financial model that keeps community programs open to a broad range of families.
periods.recommendations: Extend the successful winter fill-rate tactics by using waitlist data to add second sections for swim levels 1 through 3 and the Tuesday ceramics cohort. Continue weekly monitoring of scholarship redemptions so higher cost recovery does not mask any access gap for lower-income neighborhoods.

periods.analysis: Cost recovery rose again in 2025-Q2 to 47.8%, up 2.7 points from 45.1% in 2025-Q1, our strongest result in this sequence so far. Spring break camps, field permits at Seaport Sports Complex, and the new Saturday family literacy-and-play series all contributed to the lift. The operational story is encouraging because the gain came from participation and smarter scheduling, not from backing away from affordable entry points.
periods.recommendations: Lock in the Q2 gains by converting the highest-demand spring break camp formats into two summer cohorts at Harborview Recreation Center and North Strand Park. Direct the permits team to pre-schedule recurring field users on underused Tuesday and Thursday slots before opening single-date rentals, preserving both revenue and neighborhood access.

periods.analysis: Cost recovery eased to 45.5% in 2025-Q3, down 2.3 points from 47.8% in 2025-Q2, but remained well above the 40% target. The decline was manageable and appears tied to additional scholarship use in summer camps, heat-related aquatics schedule adjustments, and a few canceled outdoor rentals during tidal flooding days near Shoreline Green. From a resident perspective, I view this as a healthy green result: we absorbed real coastal-city operating conditions and still kept programs financially steady.
periods.recommendations: Sustain summer access by preserving the scholarship slots that drove participation, while tightening weather contingency plans for outdoor rentals at Shoreline Green and Seaport Sports Complex. Build a standing list of indoor backup spaces at Central Library, Eastbank Library, and Bayfront Community Center so paid programs can shift rather than cancel when heat or flooding interrupts schedules.

periods.analysis: In 2025-Q4, cost recovery was 43.1%, down 2.4 points from 45.5% in 2025-Q3, and still green. The seasonal cooling was expected as park rentals slowed, but we also saw higher custodial and security costs for evening events at Central Library and Bayfront Community Center. The measure remains healthy, though I want us to watch the cost side carefully so residents continue to see reliable programs without quiet erosion in service quality.
periods.recommendations: Keep the green performance stable by reviewing event staffing templates for the 15 highest-use rental rooms and matching setup hours more closely to actual booking patterns. Pilot a winter mini-series of paid indoor programs, including preschool movement, teen maker labs, and senior balance classes, at sites where staff are already scheduled.

periods.analysis: Cost recovery improved to 44.8% in 2026-Q1, up 1.7 points from 43.1% in 2025-Q4, keeping us green and back on an upward path. The winter mini-series helped, particularly teen maker labs at Eastbank Library and senior balance classes at Bayfront Community Center, and the revised room setup templates reduced avoidable labor hours. This is a practical example of operations becoming a resident outcome: cleaner cost control, fewer cancellations, and more program choices close to home.
periods.recommendations: Extend the mini-series model into spring with clear enrollment thresholds set two weeks before each start date, so staff can add sections or consolidate early. Continue the room-use staffing review monthly and share a simple dashboard with branch managers showing fill rate, direct cost, waiver participation, and net recovery by program family.

periods.analysis: Cost recovery reached 47.2% in 2026-Q2, up 2.4 points from 44.8% in 2026-Q1, nearly matching the prior high while remaining comfortably green. Strong spring field permits, expanded swim lesson cohorts, and better conversion from waitlists to paid seats all contributed to the improvement. I am especially encouraged that scholarship participation remained part of the model, because the goal is not just a good percentage; it is sustainable access for Harborview residents as the city grows.
periods.recommendations: Sustain this performance by making waitlist conversion a standard weekly task for aquatics, camps, and arts programs, with named staff owners at each major site. For the next budget cycle, use the 2025-Q2 and 2026-Q2 patterns to identify programs where adding one instructor hour or one facility block produces both more resident seats and stronger cost recovery.

periods.analysis: Program cost recovery was 37.3%, up from June’s recorded 35.9% but 2.7 percentage points below the 40% target. The improvement is real; the shortfall remains a budget pressure.
periods.recommendations: Review filled seats, waitlist conversion and program costs before changing fees. Protect scholarship access while identifying programs where additional filled seats could improve recovery.
